extracted.intended_audience: writers and producers of long-form satirical news segments (e.g., late-night writers, Last Week Tonight staff, comedy-research teams)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing ~20-minute single-topic deep-dive satirical news segments in the style of Last Week Tonight: structuring an argument, integrating research, pacing jokes, maintaining tone, and designing a closing/stunt for release and virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: LWT Format — ~20-minute single deep-dive with clear structure
rubrics_metrics.description: ~20 minutes on a single deep-dive topic. Structure: news hook → context → escalation of absurdity → call to action / button. A research team works for weeks on the deep dive; writers find jokes in the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment should be built around one topic researched over weeks. Follow the structural arc: open with a news hook to grab attention, provide context for audience understanding, escalate absurdity to expose the issue, and finish with a call to action or a distinct 'button'. Use the research as the source material for jokes rather than inventing facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as an Argument Vehicle
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece is fundamentally an ARGUMENT; the jokes are the spoonful of sugar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the argumentative core is strong: jokes should clarify, illustrate, and make the argument more palatable, not replace it. If the argument is weak, the jokes can't save it; if the jokes are weak, the argument won't reach the audience. Treat comedy as support for persuasion rather than the primary goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Why Are We Telling You This" Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Every segment must answer: why does the audience care?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on outrage alone. Define an angle the audience likely hasn't considered before so the piece adds value. Explicitly identify the 'why now' or 'why this matters to viewers' early in the piece to justify the deep dive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Density in Long-Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Pace yourself: roughly one joke per 30 seconds early, accelerating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comedy to punctuate hard information; alternate dense informational passages with comedic relief so the audience can absorb complex material. Start with a steadier joke cadence (~1 per 30s) and increase density toward climactic moments to maintain engagement through a long segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closing Bit: Release and Virality
rubrics_metrics.description: The closing bit is often a stunt (e.g., a viral product, a parody video). It functions as RELEASE after the heavy material and as a virality vehicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a closing 'button' that provides emotional or comic release and can stand alone as a shareable piece of content. The closing should relieve the audience after a heavy argument and also create material that can travel independently online to extend reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonal Discipline / Target Systems, Not Individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Cruelty to individuals is restrained even when targets deserve it; anger directed at SYSTEMS, not people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid punching down or excessively cruel jokes at vulnerable individuals. Focus critique and anger on institutions, systems, or policy actors. Maintain the boundary where comedy is the wrapper and the argument remains the core—preserve ethical/tonal discipline to retain credibility and audience trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument Robustness: Comedy-Independent Case
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the comedy be removed and the argument still stand?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the underlying facts and logic form a coherent persuasive case without jokes. If removing comedy collapses the piece, the argument is likely too reliant on humor and needs strengthening; aim for an argument that remains valid even when jokes are stripped away.
